o: For each index i we need the value of the **second** strictly greater element to the right: scan rightward, count elements strictly larger than nums[i], and the answer is the second such element (the first greater element in between is just a counter, not reported). In [2,4,0,9,6], for i=0 the greater elements to the right are 4 then 9, so answer[0]=9. For [3,3], nothing is strictly greater than 3, so both answers are -1. With n up to 1e5, an O(n^2) scan per element is too slow; we need something like O(n log n) or O(n). The key structural fact: as we sweep left to right, each new element nums[j] can serve as the *first* greater element for some pending indices and simultaneously as the *second* greater element for others.
k: Sweep left to right: when processing nums[j], it may be the first greater element for some waiting indices and the second greater element for others — promote indices between two stacks/queues.
A pair of monotonic decreasing stacks implements this promotion in amortized O(1) per element, giving O(n) total.
Alternatively, process values in decreasing order with a heap of 'seen' positions to get O(n log n).

a.i: Process indices in order of decreasing value (ties by index). When we handle index j, every previously processed index has a value >= nums[j]; those with strictly larger value already have nums[j] available as a candidate greater element. Keep a min-heap of processed indices that have found fewer than two greater elements. Pop from the heap while its top index has value strictly less than nums[j] — each pop means nums[j] is one more greater element for that index; if it's the first, keep it in a 'one-found' list, if the second, record the answer. Since equal values don't count, only pop tops with value < nums[j].
s: Create pairs (value, index), sort descending by value.
Maintain a min-heap of (index) entries whose answers are not yet finalized.

For each pair in sorted order, while heap top index has nums[top] < current value, pop it; if it had zero greater elements found, mark it as having one (push to a temp list), else set answer = nums[current].
After popping, push the current index into the heap (it now awaits its own greater elements).
Push back all temp-list indices that got their first greater element.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting plus up to n heap pushes/pops each costing O(log n).
a.sp: O(n) — heap, sorted order array, and answer array.

a.i: Sweep left to right maintaining two decreasing stacks: stack s1 holds indices that have found no greater element yet, stack s2 holds indices that have found exactly one. When we reach nums[j]: first, pop everything off s2 whose value is strictly less than nums[j] — for those indices nums[j] is their *second* greater element, so record the answer. Then pop everything off s1 whose value is strictly less than nums[j] — for those, nums[j] is their *first* greater element, so move them onto s2. Finally push j onto s1. Each index moves s1 -> s2 -> popped at most once, so total work is linear.
s: Initialize two empty stacks s1 (zero greater elements found) and s2 (one found), and answer array filled with -1.
For each j from 0 to n-1: while s2 non-empty and nums[s2.top()] < nums[j], set answer[s2.top()] = nums[j] and pop.
Collect all indices popped from s1 where nums[top] < nums[j]; push them onto s2 in the same relative order (pop into a temp list, then push reversed).
a.t: O(n) — each index is pushed and popped at most once from each stack.
a.sp: O(n) — the two stacks in the worst case (strictly decreasing input).

w: In an interview, start with the brute-force O(n^2) idea to confirm understanding, then present the double-stack solution as the optimal answer — it's clean, linear, and shows mastery of monotonic structures. The heap approach is a good fallback if you struggle to see the two-stack trick. Pitfalls: use strict inequality (<) everywhere since equal values do not count as greater ([3,3] must yield [-1,-1]); when moving indices from s1 to s2, preserve their original left-to-right order (hence the reverse step) so future pops still find the nearest valid candidates correctly; remember to initialize answers to -1. Edge cases: single-element arrays, all-equal arrays, strictly increasing arrays (answer is nums[i+2]-style shifts... actually for strictly increasing input each element's second greater is two positions ahead). Follow-ups: generalize to the k-th greater element (chain k stacks), or return indices instead of values.
